prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how technological change, the task content of work and import competition reshape labour demand, wage structures and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. The reasons are scientific. The work asks one question, what determines the demand for different kinds of labour and who bears the adjustment, and it answers with research designs that are transparent, contestable and have been repeatedly re-examined. Katz anchors the long-run skill-premium and education-versus-technology benchmark. Autor links the task and polarisation strand to the trade-shock strand. Hanson anchors the regional adjustment evidence. The core work spans roughly the early 1990s to the 2010s, so it is mature. After the chair's questions I would word the citation around the empirical findings (how labour demand shifts and how slowly and unevenly adjustment occurs). It should not claim the whole task framework or a final verdict on the size of China-shock effects. That wording handles the overlap with Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. It also answers the maturity worry, because the finding that adjustment is persistent and geographically concentrated is better established than any single magnitude. I changed one fallback. If the committee narrows the award to trade shocks, I now prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson to Autor and Hanson alone, because a narrowed citation makes omitting Dorn hard to defend. I also changed my alternatives, replacing B003 with B037. B003's identification and coding problems and the Vishny gap weigh more heavily on it than I weighted them in my opening. B037 has the cleanest attribution among the macro candidates.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is that B038 may be two achievements joined by shared authorship, technology and wage structure on one side and trade shocks on the other. Under the three-name cap, any choice then excludes a real contributor, Dorn in the trio I propose and Katz in the Autor-Dorn-Hanson version. The task framework also has priority claims outside the ballot (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu), and the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes are neighbouring. China-shock magnitudes and shift-share identification remain debated. I cannot rule out that a committee finds B044's single originating model, with its two-name credit, easier to defend than my trio. That would be a legitimate judgement and not a scientific error on either side.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and B038 third. She gives B038 less weight on maturity because China-shock persistence and shift-share identification are still debated, and she says she would support B038 if the committee found a convincing way to credit Dorn.
responses.response: I take the Dorn condition seriously, and it is why I have moved my fallback to Autor-Dorn-Hanson for a trade-only citation. I still prefer the trio with Katz for a labour-demand citation, because Katz's strand is what lets the prize speak to technology and not only to import competition. On maturity I partly agree. The magnitude and long-run persistence of the effects are contested, but the qualitative finding of slow, concentrated adjustment has been replicated and extended by many groups for over a decade. A citation built on the finding and not on a point estimate leans on the mature part of the evidence. I have not independently re-verified that literature, and I accept that this is a judgement about wording, not a settled fact.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B044 first. Her objection to B038 is that its credit boundary is blurred by Acemoglu's neighbouring prize and by the two strands, and she wants an argument about which strand carries the discovery. She also told me she would not rank B003 above B044 until the identification critiques are answered.
responses.response: On B003 we agree, which is why I have dropped it from my alternatives. On B038 I answer your question directly. The discovery is the empirical establishment of how technology and trade shift labour demand, and the strands share designs and a set of authors. The 2024 prize concerned institutions and prosperity, so Acemoglu's recognition does not cover the task-and-trade empirics. The priority gap on the task framework is real and a citation limited to the empirical contribution acknowledges it. I concede that your point about B044 has force. Melitz (2003) is a more singular origin, and B038's boundary will always involve a judgement call that B044's does not. Whether that outweighs B038's breadth is where we differ. I do not think it is a difference about scientific quality.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B037 with Kiyotaki and Moore. He left B038 out of his configuration because the boundary looks unstable (his opening proposed only Autor and Hanson) and Katz's skill-biased-change work is adjacent to Goldin's 2023 prize. He said he would revisit it if a principled boundary can be agreed.
responses.response: My attempt at a principled boundary is this. The award is for the empirical evidence on how technology and trade shift labour demand, with each name anchoring a documented strand and Dorn's omission acknowledged openly. On Goldin, I read the 2023 citation as covering women's labour-market outcomes, not the wage-structure and education-versus-technology evidence, so I count it as adjacency and a modest timing consideration and not duplication. I agree that B037 has the cleaner attribution, and I hold that as a real advantage. Where I differ is the empirical side. You and Strömberg both accept that the collateral-amplification channel is mostly confirmed through calibrated models, and for me that weighs somewhat against B037's maturity. I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Krusell opened with B017 and now prefers B044. He proposed Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B038 and doubts that the skill-premium and trade-shock literatures are one discovery. He says the task framework has contributors outside the list.
responses.response: I concede that the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio is the tightest bounded award, and that it is the right trio if the committee decides the discovery is trade shocks. I differ on whether that is the best reading. A prize that credits only the trade-shock papers drops the older and more foundational wage-structure analysis that those papers are written against. If the committee does split the strands, I would no longer take Autor and Hanson alone as my fallback, since I think Dorn would then belong. On the contested boundary of the task framework I agree with you that the citation should say what it recognises and nothing broader.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B037 and lists B038 as his first alternative. He notes that Katz also appears on B045, so any B038 award should state which of Katz's contributions it recognises. He also says that more weight on direct empirical confirmation would favour B038 over B037.
responses.response: I accept the Katz point and would write it into the citation. His credit here is the long-run skill-premium and education-versus-technology analysis, and the intergenerational-mobility work on B045 is a separate candidate that I do not credit under B038. On direct confirmation, I agree that is a difference between B038 and B037, but I would not lean on it alone, since a clean theoretical mechanism that disciplines a literature is itself a prize-worthy contribution. I weigh it as one consideration among attribution, maturity and scope. I do not treat our agreement on what B037 lacks as evidence about B037's merit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees B038 as one achievement on labour demand or two strands, and so whether the third name should be Katz or Dorn. Under a narrowed trade-shock citation I would support Autor-Dorn-Hanson, and I would not support Autor-Hanson alone.

How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 neighbouring prizes should lower the marginal case. My view is that adjacency counts only when the earlier citation covered the same discovery, and I would apply that standard equally to B044, B038, B037 and B017.

The size and persistence of China-shock effects and the validity of shift-share identification. I have not independently verified the current literature, and my judgement of maturity rests on my own knowledge and colleagues' statements.

Why B044 is not my first choice. The reasons are the uncredited work of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and welfare magnitudes that depend on functional-form assumptions. The 2008 prize is not a reason. I would find B044 an acceptable outcome if B038 cannot reach six votes, on the grounds of its clean originating model and its long confirmation in firm-level data.

Whether B037's empirical support is thin enough to count against it, and whether Gertler and Gilchrist belong in a single achievement. I have not checked the boundary against the 2022 scientific background.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, with no change. The supplied profile documents no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn, to Melitz and Helpman, or to Kiyotaki and Moore. My disclosed connections are my SSE affiliation with committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, my Lund colleagues, and my co-authors in matching, auctions and market design. None of these involves the credited names on B038, B044 or B037. I do not think any disclosed tie requires me to limit my participation on a ballot. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
